title: Superpowers, Bipolarity and the Cold War

cards.h: The 45-year contest that shaped the modern world
cards.b:
The Cold War (c. 1947-1991) was a struggle between the United States and the Soviet Union that never became a direct war. It shaped alliances, arms races, decolonisation, the UN and India's own foreign policy.

It matters for the exam in three ways. First, it is the base for bipolarity, a key idea in IR theory (Waltz). Second, it explains why India chose non-alignment. Third, its end in 1991 opened the "unipolar moment" and set India's economic reforms.

Expect questions on origins, major crises, détente, the end of the Cold War, and the debate among historians. Stay with dates and doctrines: Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, NATO, Warsaw Pact, Cuban Missile Crisis, SALT, Helsinki, INF Treaty.

Remember the Indian lens: Nehru, Bandung, the 1971 Indo-Soviet treaty, and the post-1991 recalibration.

The US and USSR fought together against Nazi Germany, but their systems and goals differed: liberal capitalism and democracy versus Communist one-party rule.

  • Yalta (February 1945) and Potsdam (July-August 1945): wartime conferences. Disputes over Poland, Germany and Eastern Europe grew.
  • 1946. George Kennan's "Long Telegram" from Moscow (February) urged firm resistance to Soviet expansion. Churchill's "Iron Curtain" speech at Fulton, Missouri (March).
  • 1947. The Truman Doctrine (12 March): US aid to Greece and Turkey, and support for free peoples resisting subjugation. Kennan's "X" article in Foreign Affairs set out containment. The Marshall Plan (announced June 1947) gave about $13 billion in aid to rebuild Western Europe. The USSR formed the Cominform (September) and Andrei Zhdanov described a world of "two camps".
  • 1948-49. Berlin blockade and airlift (June 1948 to May 1949). NATO founded on 4 April 1949 with 12 members.

• 1949. USSR tests its first atomic bomb (August). Communists win in China (October).
  • 1950-53. Korean War. A UN force led by the US faced North Korea and China. India chaired the Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission.
  • 1955. West Germany joins NATO; the USSR forms the Warsaw Pact (May).
  • 1956. The USSR crushes the Hungarian uprising. The Suez crisis shows the limits of old European powers; the US and USSR both pressured Britain and France.
  • 1957. Sputnik starts the space race.
  • 1961. The Berlin Wall is built (August).
  • 1962. The Cuban Missile Crisis (October, 13 days): the USSR placed missiles in Cuba, the US imposed a naval "quarantine", and the crisis ended with Soviet withdrawal and a US pledge not to invade Cuba, plus the quiet removal of US missiles from Turkey. It was the closest the world came to nuclear war.

Result: a hotline (1963) and the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963).

Historians split the era into phases. Each had its own mood, from fear and crisis to cooperation and then a tense revival.

Use this as a quick frame in answers. It helps you place events and show you see the pattern: crisis, learning, arms control, relapse, and finally collapse of one side.

cards.h: Détente and the second Cold War
cards.b:
Détente (1969-79) was a relaxation of tension.

  • 1969-72. Nixon and Kissinger opened ties with China (Nixon's visit, February 1972), and played the "China card". Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik improved West German ties with the East.
  • 1972. SALT I and the ABM Treaty were signed in Moscow.
  • 1975. The Helsinki Final Act (CSCE) accepted post-war borders and added human rights language that dissidents later used.

Détente broke down after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (December 1979), the Iranian Revolution and US reaction. Under Reagan, the US raised arms spending, supported mujahideen, and announced the Strategic Defense Initiative (1983), called "Star Wars". This is the "Second Cold War" (1979-85).

Meanwhile the Third World saw proxy wars: Vietnam (US withdrew 1973; Saigon fell 1975), Angola, Ethiopia, Nicaragua and Afghanistan.

Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in March 1985. He brought glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring), and "new thinking" in foreign policy.

  • December 1987. The INF Treaty eliminated a whole class of US and Soviet missiles.
  • 1989. The USSR withdrew from Afghanistan (February). Eastern European regimes fell. The Berlin Wall opened on 9 November.
  • 1990. German reunification (3 October).
  • July 1991. The Warsaw Pact was dissolved, and START I was signed.
  • December 1991. The Soviet Union dissolved, with Gorbachev resigning on 25 December.

Why did it end? Debated answers: Soviet economic stagnation and overreach; US pressure under Reagan; Gorbachev's reforms and choice not to use force; nationalism within the USSR; the power of ideas (constructivists). Realists were surprised, which fed the criticism of neorealism.

cards.h: How historians explain the Cold War
cards.b:
Orthodox (traditional)

Soviet expansion started it and the US responded defensively. Herbert Feis and Arthur Schlesinger Jr.

Revisionist

US capitalism needed open markets and pushed the USSR into a corner. William Appleman Williams, The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959); Gabriel Kolko; Walter LaFeber.

Post-revisionist

Both sides contributed, through fear, misperception and domestic politics. John Lewis Gaddis, The Long Peace (1986) and We Now Know (1997), using new Soviet archives, put more weight on Stalin. Melvyn Leffler emphasised US security fears.

Why no war? Kenneth Waltz argued bipolarity was stable. Others credit nuclear deterrence, mutual assured destruction (MAD), and rules of the game after Cuba. Gaddis called it the "long peace".

Cold War was cold only at the centre. In Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan and Africa, millions died in proxy wars.

• Two superpowers far ahead in military power and nuclear arsenals.
  • Blocs and alliances: NATO (1949), Warsaw Pact (1955), SEATO (1954) and CENTO (the Baghdad Pact, 1955).
  • Nuclear deterrence and the arms race. Global stockpiles peaked at over 60,000 warheads in the mid-1980s.
  • Ideological contest: liberal capitalism versus Marxism-Leninism.
  • Proxy wars and spheres of influence: Truman Doctrine; the Brezhnev Doctrine (1968) after the invasion of Czechoslovakia.
  • Economic blocs: Marshall Plan and the OEEC; the Soviet side had COMECON (1949), covered in the next unit.
  • Third World choice: join a bloc or stay non-aligned.

The UN Security Council was often paralysed by vetoes. Only a few operations, such as in Korea (1950, helped by a Soviet boycott), went ahead.

• Non-alignment. Nehru chose independence from both blocs. India stayed out of SEATO and CENTO and criticised pacts. See the next lesson.
  • Korea. India mediated and chaired the Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission (1953), and sent a medical unit and a custodian force.
  • US-Pakistan ties. Pakistan joined SEATO and the Baghdad Pact, and got US arms. India worried.
  • Soviet ties. The USSR vetoed UN action on Kashmir in the 1950s-60s and supported India's industrialisation (Bhilai steel plant). The Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation (August 1971) came as the US and China leaned to Pakistan before the Bangladesh war.
  • 1962. India sought help from the US during the Sino-Indian war, which coincided with the Cuban crisis.
  • 1979-89. India's muted response to the Soviet entry into Afghanistan drew criticism.
  • After 1991. The loss of the Soviet partner, plus the balance-of-payments crisis, pushed India toward economic reform and a "Look East" policy, and improved ties with the US.

"Trace the origins of the Cold War. Which explanation do you find convincing?"
"Bipolarity was more stable than the present multipolar world." Discuss.
"What were the causes of the end of the Cold War?"
"Examine India's response to the Cold War."

Structure: context (1945), then origins with Kennan, Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan. Add crisis dates, détente (SALT, Helsinki), second Cold War, and end (INF, 1989, 1991). Put historians in a three-box list. Add Waltz on stability. Close with India: non-alignment, Korea, 1971 treaty, 1991 shift.

A timeline diagram with 8 dates adds clarity and saves words.
